“In reality, however, once a given elevation has been reached, the measurable weight of air passed through in any further ascent does not increase proportionately to the additional height—as the preceding remarks plainly show—but according to a continually diminishing ratio. Hence it is clear that, however high we rise, we cannot literally reach a boundary beyond which atmosphere ceases to exist. Air must remain, I reasoned, though in a condition of infinite attenuation.

“On the other side, I knew that arguments had been advanced for an actual, definite atmospheric boundary, with absolutely no air beyond it. Yet one circumstance neglected by advocates of that boundary appeared to deserve the most earnest inquiry, even if it did not positively disprove their doctrine. Compare the intervals separating successive returns of Encke’s comet to perihelion, allowing with the utmost precision for every disturbance caused by planetary attraction: the periods prove to be gradually shortening. In other words, the major axis of its elliptical orbit decreases slowly but with perfect regularity. This is exactly what should occur if the comet encountered resistance from an exceedingly thin ethereal substance filling the regions through which it travelled. Such a medium, by diminishing the comet’s speed, must evidently strengthen its centripetal force through weakening the centrifugal. Put otherwise, the sun’s attraction would steadily gain influence, drawing the comet closer with each revolution. Indeed, no other explanation accounts for the observed change. Moreover, the true diameter of the same comet’s nebulous envelope is seen to shrink rapidly as it nears the sun and to expand just as rapidly on its journey towards aphelion. Was I not warranted in agreeing with M. Valz that this apparent reduction in volume arose from pressure exerted by the ethereal medium already described, which grows denser only according to its nearness to the sun? The lens-shaped appearance called the zodiacal light also merited consideration. This glow, conspicuous in tropical regions and impossible to confuse with meteoric brightness, stretches diagonally upward from the horizon, generally following the direction of the solar equator. To me it clearly suggested a thin atmosphere spreading outward from the sun, at least beyond Venus’s orbit and, I believed, indefinitely farther. Certainly I could not imagine this medium limited either to the comet’s elliptical path or to the sun’s immediate vicinity.

After sending them in, I could not stay away from the places that held them. I felt as though the petitions had better chances and were less hopeless when I was nearby. Driven by this irrational restlessness and distress, I wandered the streets in the evening, passing the offices and houses where I had left them. Even now, London’s dreary western streets on a cold, dusty spring night, with their stern rows of closed mansions and long lines of lamps, make me sad because of that association.

My daily visits to him were now shorter, and he was guarded more strictly. Seeing—or imagining—that they suspected I might bring him poison, I asked to be searched before sitting beside his bed. I told the officer who was always present that I would do anything to reassure him that my intentions were entirely innocent. Nobody treated either of us unkindly. They performed their duty, but without harshness. The officer always told me his condition had worsened. Other sick prisoners in the room, and those serving as their nurses—criminals, but still capable of kindness, thank God—always confirmed it.

As the days passed, I increasingly noticed him lying quietly, looking at the white ceiling. His face seemed without light until something I said brightened it for a moment; then the brightness faded again. Sometimes he could barely speak, or could not speak at all. Then he answered by pressing my hand gently, and I learned to understand him very well.

On the tenth day, I found him more changed than ever. His eyes were fixed on the door and lit up when I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said as I sat beside the bed, “I thought you were late. But I knew you couldn’t be.”

“It’s exactly the right time,” I told him. “I waited at the gate.”

“You always wait at the gate, don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So I won’t lose a moment.”

“Thank you, dear boy, thank you. God bless you! You’ve never abandoned me, dear boy.”

I squeezed his hand without speaking, unable to forget that I had once intended to abandon him.

“And best of all,” he said, “you’ve felt more at ease with me since this dark cloud came over me than you did when the sun was shining.

“If you want one for home use, though, I can provide an excellent device and promise you will be pleased with the result. May I ask who it is for? If you mean to use it against the police or anyone at Scotland Yard, I’m afraid I cannot help. English detectives are really our greatest friends. I’ve always found that, by counting on their stupidity, we can do exactly as we please. I couldn’t bear to lose one.”

“I assure you,” Lord Arthur replied, “the police have nothing to do with it. The clock is actually for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Goodness! I didn’t realize you had such strong feelings about religion, Lord Arthur. Very few young men do these days.”

“I’m afraid you give me too much credit, Herr Winckelkopf,” Lord Arthur said, blushing. “I really know nothing about theology.”

“Then this is entirely a private affair?”

“Entirely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged and left the room. A few minutes later, he returned with a round piece of dynamite about the size of a penny and a pretty little French clock. On top stood a gilded bronze figure of Liberty trampling the many-headed monster of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face lit up. “That is exactly what I need,” he exclaimed. “Now, tell me how it explodes.”

“Ah, that is my secret,” Herr Winckelkopf answered, studying his invention with understandable pride. “Tell me when you want it to explode, and I will set it for that precise moment.”

“Well, today is Tuesday. If you could send it immediately—”

“Impossible. I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends in Moscow. Still, I could perhaps send it tomorrow.”

“Oh, that will be quite soon enough,” Lord Arthur said politely, “provided it arrives tomorrow evening or Thursday morning. For the explosion, let us say exactly noon on Friday. The Dean is always home then.”

“Friday at noon,” Herr Winckelkopf repeated, writing it in a large account book on a desk beside the fireplace.

“And now,” Lord Arthur said, standing, “please tell me how much I owe you.”

“It is such a small job that I would rather not charge for it. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and delivery about five shillings. I am delighted to help any friend of Count Rouvaloff.”

“But what about your time and trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?
